title: Is Instinct safe to use? Three things to know before you sign up

reading.body:
Instinct, an AI personal assistant, uses personal data shared with it to train its models by default, requiring users to actively opt out rather than opt in. The system retains copies of data even after users disconnect connected accounts like Gmail, making full data removal difficult. This represents a deployment choice to prioritize model training over user control of sensitive information like browsing habits, location, health details, and financial records.

The assistant can make purchases on users' behalf with shared payment methods, with mistaken or unintended purchases attributed legally to the user rather than the company. This compounds the privacy risk by adding financial risk to the data collection model. A human review step before purchase execution, or a requirement for explicit authorization per transaction, could have prevented unintended charges from being treated as user liability.

It is not established whether these design choices reflect Instinct's terms of service disclosures, user awareness levels, or the basis for Norton's safety assessment relative to its own product.

reports.title: Is Instinct safe to use? Three things to know before you sign up

summary:
# Summary

Instinct, a popular new AI personal assistant, presents significant privacy and security risks that users should understand before signing up. By default, Instinct uses personal information shared with the assistant to train its AI models unless users actively opt out, meaning sensitive data like browsing habits, location, health details, and financial information could be used without direct authorization. Additionally, even when users disconnect connected accounts like Gmail, Instinct retains copies of previously indexed data and continues storing it in its records, making it difficult to fully remove personal information.

Beyond data collection concerns, Instinct can make purchases on users' behalf using shared payment methods, and any unintended or mistaken purchases are legally attributed to the user rather than the company. Norton contrasts its own Family Assistant product as a safer alternative, emphasizing that it does not use shared data to train AI models, requires explicit user consent before taking actions, and allows easy data deletion. The article stresses that while AI assistants offer convenience, users should not have to sacrifice privacy and security to benefit from these tools.
